INTRODUCTION

1992: - Jubilee Year

- Centenary of the Constitutions

Among the many initiatives planned by the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne for a worthy celebration of its 125th anniversary is the publication of Mother Rosa's Letters of the four years 1871-1874, in two volumes (following the first, published in 1990). These letters bring us into the dynamic fervour of the early days, into the heart of the original charism as it was being realised in works of charity and becoming history through Mother Rosa, Fr. Tornatore and the first Daughters of Saint Anne.

Mother Rosa offered herself to the charism, let it permeate her to the roots of her being and, under the impulse of the Holy Spirit, directed her life towards it in being and in action. Fr. Tornatore, under the impulse and enlightenment of the same Spirit, set out that charism explicitly in the «1869 Rule», making it visible and assimilable for the Daughters of Saint Anne. Mother Rosa recognised in that Rule the faithful expression of the Institute's spirit, the instrument of fundamental importance for forming the Religious, and the document on which the Church relies to recognise God's action in the new institution and give it the seal of authenticity. So she worked with eager care and prompt action, amply witnessed by these letters, to have that Rule approved by the Church. But for her and Fr. Tornatore the approval process was a long season of sowing in tears, through the at first very troubled phases of 1871-1874 and the following years of slow, painful waiting, culminating in final approval on 26 July 1892 — exactly a hundred years ago. This happy anniversary converges with the celebration of the Jubilee Year proposed by the 18th General Chapter as a «memorial» that makes the past present and projects it into the future. Both anniversaries point back to the gushing springs of the origins, to the gift represented by Mother Rosa and Fr. Tornatore; charism and Rule: a vital richness, a harmonious and integrating reality looking to the future: God's Work, the heavenly Father's plan, always open to the universal dimensions of the Kingdom; a plan that awaits our commitment to take up today the challenges of history with the same radicalism as Mother Rosa and the first Sisters.

Mother Rosa's letters and their historical, autobiographical and relational value

As was said in the preface to the first volume (1864-1870), the letters, through their historical, spiritual and charismatic value, are documents and an important part of the Family's heritage; they belong to its life in its origins, growth and development through time. They offer its «memory»; they point back, as to a source of light, to the particular charism given by the Father to the vital dynamism of the Foundress and, through her, to other lives. Mother Rosa, entrusted with the charism, in welcoming it experienced its irresistible driving force, became aware of it and let herself be guided, urged by the «charity that does violence to her inmost being», and, attentive to the needs of her brothers and sisters, became a response of love in concrete works. Other lives were drawn into her orbit and formed the Family, which she calls God's Work, little plant of the Church, field; images that express theologically a living organism sharing in the life and mystery of the Church and becoming in it a history of salvation. Of this organism growing in space and time the letters are a faithful mirror. By their specifically social and relational nature they give clear and authentic information about Mother Rosa in the many and varied relationships belonging to the Family in its spiritual and practical reality. It is always and only she, Mother Rosa, who presents herself in the letters and expresses herself in her essence while, adhering to the Father's will, she carries out the mission he has asked and goes on asking of her day after day: to live the charism essentially herself, to nourish her Daughters with it and help them live it in harmony with their personal gifts and aspirations; to spread it in the Church through the service of a generous charity nourished by prayer and fraternal communion which, in filial union with the Eternal Father, becomes a balm of consolation and liberation for others.

The letters of 1871-1874 also have their own originality and value. Belonging to the early period of the Family, they not only reveal and transmit its bursting vitality, finding room to grow in many vocations, but are also shot through with the travail over the Rule in its most critical and acute phases. A travail of tears and pain for the Mother; fruitful for her, who through contradiction took it on with stronger awareness, defended it and saved it; fruitful for us, who receive it in its most genuine identity.

1871-1874: plans and reality

With 1871 the Institute entered its fifth year. The «little plant» had put out its shoots and two «branch houses» were also growing, one in Piacenza, the other in Genoa. Blessed by God with new vocations, blessed by the Holy Father, to whom the text of the Rule, printed with the approval of the Bishop of Piacenza, had been presented (L 86). A very small family, Mother Rosa's and Fr. Tornatore's, confined to narrow limits. It would certainly grow in time. But growth, expansion, the how and the where belong to God. Rosa knows this. In the nights spent in prayer in «her little room», where she takes refuge alone with the Spouse, her gaze ranges further, over the whole world. God's Work will be great, because it is God's. The goal is therefore high, for God's Plan can only be a dynamic opening to the future, the more, the beyond. Of that plan she, a poor little «nothing», is the faithful instrument offered without reserve: «For God's Work I offered myself as a victim», and all of herself — mind, will, heart — is actively directed towards the one pole: God's will in his Work.

Starting from an assessment of the Institute's situation and looking with faith to its future, she conceived a plan and a well-structured programme, in harmony — she was convinced — with God's will.

  • She would see to the founding of new houses and, in each of them, train the sisters in the very field of work, by an active, experiential method, through common life, prayer and charitable action.

  • Father Tornatore would devote himself full time at the Mother House to its direction and to the formation of the Sisters.

  • Both would work to press for approval of the Rule, going to Rome if necessary.

The first step therefore concerned Fr. Tornatore. She reflected and prayed at length, asked friends for advice and prayers (Lettere 1, L. 156; 254; 269), consulted Bishop Mgr. Ranza and, supported by his letters of recommendation, asked the Superior General of the Lazarists to place Fr. Tornatore under his direct jurisdiction so that, subject only to him and not to the local Superior, he could devote himself entirely to the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne (L 5; Ind. III, 2).

She then went to Sampierdarena and stayed there almost without a break from February to April (L. 13-51), carrying out the part of the programme belonging to her. She was with the sisters, encouraging, guiding and enlightening them by the witness of her life and by suitable meditations and talks on religious and formative subjects, and with practical instructions and lessons for the nurses. She prayed and worked alongside them. She also worked to open a new house and on 17 April 1871 began home nursing of the sick in Genoa (Cf. Ind. IV). She also invited Fr. Tornatore to visit the two communities.

Second step. Towards the end of May she went to Rome with Fr. Tornatore, Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino and Carlotta. Fr. Agostino Donadio was expecting them. A good friend and expert in Roman life, he directed them to the right people to obtain what they hoped for. Mother Rosa, already disappointed by the Superior General's negative answer about Fr. Tornatore (L 42, n. 2), learned that nothing had been done about the Constitutions. She asked for a private audience with the Holy Father and humbly presented to him «the text of the Constitutions» and a «petition» that Fr. Tornatore «might act freely» in the Institute (L 63). On that same day, 4 June 1871, the Institute was assigned a Cardinal Protector, the Archbishop of Ferrara, Luigi Vannicelli Casoni. From him and his most worthy secretary, Mgr. Mariano Wanstienkist, Mother Rosa received marks of goodwill, esteem, help and comfort.

She left Rome in the firmest hope that the Rule would soon be examined and approved.

Meanwhile another foundation took shape, at Ferrara, through the interest and wish of Countess Maria Anna Trotti (L. 84; 101).

She took the Sisters there and stayed as long as was needed for a good start (L. 107-123). From there, longed for and awaited by the Sisters, she went to the other communities: Piacenza, Genoa, Sampierdarena (L. 125-148). In January 1872 she was still travelling; with Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino she began another work at Nizza Monferrato, which would include almost all the activities in the Institute's general plan: nursing the sick in the town hospital and at home, school for girls and boys, catechism (L. 153-157).

At this point a serious obstacle arose on the road to the Rule.

The travail over the Rule (1871-1874)

The friends in Rome — Fr. Agostino Donadio, Fr. Giuseppe Manfredini, Mgr. Mariano Wanstienkist, Mgr. Domenico Tellarini — who had assured the Mother and Fr. Tornatore of their interest in the Rule, followed its course closely and with careful attention kept them informed, encouraging them to hope. The letters exchanged between Rome and Piacenza in this period document the affair in its various phases, from its calm beginning to later setbacks caused by doubts, negative judgements and unfavourable decisions. Mother

Rosa's letters express not only the facts but her personal involvement; with her characteristic spontaneity she reveals her moods, feelings, will-power to achieve the good cause, and unshakeable firmness in defending the spirit of the Rule.

The first significant news came from Mgr. Wanstienkist on 18 July 1871: «I foresee changes», reinforced with a worse note on the 29th of the same month by Mgr. Tellarini: «The disputed points concern the extrinsic more than the intrinsic». On 1 August Fr. Manfredini wrote to Fr. Tornatore: «On the matter of the Rule I cannot give you good news... many things are being said against it, I don't know how... I have heard it called too rigid». On the 13th Fr. Agostino wrote to Mother Rosa: «Yesterday I visited Mgr. Vitelleschi, the new secretary (of the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars), and we talked at length about the Rule... and he told me that with that Rule you will never see your Institute approved and that in his opinion you should withdraw it from all the houses, and that I should write this to my good Mother...». Mother Rosa felt the harshness of this reality: «It was a cruel blow for me», but did not grasp the full import of the sad news. She was so convinced of the goodness of the Rule that she answered Fr. Agostino: «...and yet it will be that one — she says — in the end everyone will be convinced» (L 113). On 16 November it was Fr. Manfredini who gave more sad news: «The Consultor's vote is against approval of the Rule, not as to substance but as to form», and he suggested corrections: «Rewrite the Rule from the beginning as an analytical index...».

Fr. Tornatore set to work, making the recommended changes (L 144). His work was sent to Fr. Manfredini, who replied: «I have set about the Rule you sent me and I hope you will allow me to remove all that (words only, though) which I know sounds harsh to those gentlemen, learned perhaps, but little versed in the spirit of gospel perfection». But this letter also contained a warning of the great tribulation that 1872, now at the door, held for them all: «The Rule submitted to the S. Congregation has been passed by it to the Holy Office». The good Father seemed not to realise how serious this step was. The saddest news fell to Mgr. Wanstienkist. On 17 February he wrote to Mother Rosa: «The S. Congregation does not admit the Rule in the form and substance in which it was compiled; all copies... must be withdrawn by the ecclesiastical Authorities from whoever has them, so that the said printed copies may be torn up. It further orders that the author, whoever he may be, and its supporters and propagators be removed and kept away from any interference in or direction of the said Institute».

For Mother Rosa the blow was mortal. Her well-designed plan collapsed, undermined at its foundations, a plan for whose fulfilment she had conceived the fairest hopes. She had wanted, and worked with all her strength and every possible means, for Fr. Tornatore to be able to devote himself full time to the Family of Saint Anne, whose spirit he shared, having expressed it wonderfully in the Rule. Now he was taken away entirely from the Family and from her. She was dismayed: «What struck me was not so much hearing what the S. Congregation had decided about the Rule as reading that the one who was its true founder is removed» (L 171). But she bowed her head and obeyed: «God's will be done... I adore all his dispositions and submit to the will of the Church» (ibid.).

She went to Rome and on arrival hastened to contact the people in charge of the case. She was told again what she already knew, and more besides. Day by day she told everything to the faithful Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, in her usual telegraphic style, with deliberate hints and the promise of later explanations: «All by word of mouth».

«Yesterday they gave me the mortal blow: deprived of everything, I cannot write to that person (Fr. Tornatore), and I am required to compile the Rule under the direction of the Bishop of Ferrara» (L 178). «...I hope I have found out everything; I think this martyrdom is crueller than the guillotine» (ibid.). «...Today I am going to the Holy Office. On Monday I shall have a private audience with the Holy Father and leave at once for Ferrara» (L. 183; 185). «I have spoken with the Holy Father. On seeing me he laughed several times: ah! ah! the Daughters of Saint Anne, the Daughters of Saint Anne! He shook my hand and I was able to say everything. Holding his hand, I begged him; in the end I was very happy, as the first time and perhaps more» (L 185). «...The storm is about to calm down» (ibid.). «Mgr. Vitelleschi arranged everything very well» (L 181). She gave Mgr. Ranza an exact account of what had happened: «On arriving in Rome I spoke at once with His Eminence Cardinal Vannicelli, who sent me to Mgr. Vitelleschi; this is what that holy Prelate told me: that for the reform of the Rule they will entrust me to His Excellency Mgr. Giordani, and that His Holiness wishes this Institute, which does so much good, to be consolidated... I have already spoken with Mgr. ... He leaves on Sunday for Ferrara and I am going to join him» (L 184). She also wrote news of this to friends and benefactors: Countesses Isabella Caracciolo (L 180) and Maria Anna Trotti (L 181). At Ferrara she came to an agreement with Mgr. Giordani and drew up a precise work plan, which she reported to Cardinal Vannicelli (L 189) and Mgr. Vitelleschi (L 190), expressing her deepest gratitude to them, as also to Mgr. Wanstienkist (L 193). She then visited the individual communities to see how they were going, because, as Mgr. Vitelleschi had suggested, «she must draw the Constitutions from observance». After a month of visits and various commitments (L. 195-210) she was at last in Ferrara (L 211). She devoted herself to the Rule without counting time or sparing her strength. She told Mgr. Vitelleschi: «I have already written a good part of the Constitutions, keeping to your obedience and drawing them from pure observance» (L 212). On 26 April she had finished: «Last night I finished reorganising the Rule — she announced to Mgr. Ranza — it will soon be revised by His Eminence and sent by him to the S. Congregation» (L 219); and to Mgr. Vitelleschi: «Today I handed the manuscript of the Constitutions to His Eminence for the necessary observations» (L 220). In patient expectation of the revision, «to which the Cardinal is devoting himself with untiring zeal» (L 225), a wait that seemed too long to her (L 245), she asked, with an eye to «afterwards», whether she would have to go to Rome (L 231).

At last, on 18 June, the Constitutions were sent to Rome (L 267). The next day she returned to Piacenza, her soul relieved of a great weight but not entirely free of fear about the outcome; nor were her sufferings, her dear travelling companions, lacking. In Piacenza her presence was called for because of «the many matters and in particular the acceptance of many postulants» (L 266); then she would have to visit the other communities. There was never any lack of work; what she lacked was «health, so desperate that every moment she needs support to stay on her feet» (L 280, to Fr. Agostino Donadio); «one thing alone comforts me and assures me that what I suffer is God's will: seeing the Lord's Work grow stronger every day and sail ahead in full sail» (L 266). She spent the remaining months of that memorable 1872 shuttling between the houses: in September she was in Genoa, Piacenza and Nizza Monferrato; in October back to Nizza, then Genoa; in November again to Nizza, then to the Mother House.

Here the news reached her, from the Cardinal Protector, of the new rejection. The second draft would not do either, Mgr. Wanstienkist wrote, ending his letter with the negative decision: «It is absolutely necessary to compose others», and with Mgr. Vitelleschi's suggestions for a possible quick solution: «To reach a conclusion, one could have taken as a norm the Rule of the Dorotheans for the education of girls... and for nursing the sick and running hospitals the Rule of the Franciscans called Stigmatines... With these two guides the Rule of the Daughters of Saint Anne should be put together, making the changes thought necessary, and to draw up this Rule the holy and learned Jesuit Fr. Fava would be very suitable».

The Mother could not accept this solution. «Keep the spirit firm», the Holy Father had commanded her; nor could she hurry to Rome, being very ill. But she asked the Cardinal Protector that Fr. Fava go «to the Mother House to observe the whole way of life and form the Constitutions on that basis» (L 329).

She was soon reassured: Fr. Fava would deal with the Rule without looking at those of other Institutes and would take its spirit from the unapproved Rule submitted to the S. Congregation, which would be given to him as a special favour (L 334). As soon as she could she went to Rome again. To the aim of hastening approval another, far more pressing, had been added: to defend and clarify the spirit of the Institute; and a third as well: to open a house in Rome, a long-cherished wish (L. 56, n. 2; 61, n. 4; 101; 245). She learned first of all that Fr. Fava, because of his many commitments, could not attend to the Rule straight away. After waiting almost two months, to overcome the obstacle and safeguard the authenticity of the Institute's spirit, the Mother asked Mgr. Vitelleschi to «join two other servants of God to Fr. Fava and that these might have the goodness and charity to listen to me, because if he gives a new spirit to the Rule, it would no longer be our Institute» (26 March 1873). She also asked him to intercede kindly so that Fr. Tornatore might again take care of the Institute (ibid.). And again on 7 April, having taken the courageous decision to withdraw through the Cardinal Protector the Constitutions still lying among Fr. Fava's many papers, she wrote to him again: «I send you the latest Constitutions, which the most pious Rev. Father has not yet been able to deal with... Cardinal Vannicelli gave them to me and I place them in your hands, so that you may kindly pass them to one or two consultors... I would wish them to have the charity to listen to me if there are any observations to be made». Why such haste? one might object. She repeats it in the same letter with the passion that burned in her soul: «Your Most Rev. Excellency, you cannot believe how much pain this affair causes me, having so many religious to instruct in this spirit and nothing, neither printed nor in manuscript; I ask it of you for pity's sake». The revision was entrusted to Father Raimondo Bianchi, Master General of the Dominicans.

Reassured again on this essential aspect of her programme, she could take up the other: Fr. Tornatore's readmission. She went up and down many stairs, explaining to the people «who mattered» the reasons for and value of his presence for the orderly and fruitful development of the Institute, both in temporal matters and in the direction and formation of genuine Daughters of Saint Anne. On 24 April 1873 she confided to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa that she had met with considerable difficulties that day because of the Father, and concluded bitterly: «How many enemies he has! I thought I would burst with grief, my God!». The same day she had appealed to Cardinal Costantino Patrizi, Vicar of Pius IX: «If Your Eminence would call this Priest and, giving him orders and obediences, then allow him at least to take care of those two houses in Piacenza!».

Mother Rosa's letters are silent on both «matters» during the remaining months of 1873. But in January 1874 some fleeting hints reveal a certain anxiety about the Rule. She went to Rome again in January. She asked for prayers that «she might obtain everything» from Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini (16 January); to her friend Anna Grasso she wrote: «I am in great tribulations» (18 January); to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa (on the 17th): «Tomorrow is the day of the consistory for me» (that is, of the plenary session of the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars). On the 20th to the same: «I hope we shall soon have light; my blood is about to rot, you can imagine why. What suffering! Ah, everything is going from bad to worse; God alone is for us; (men) — how horrible, my dear, just to think of it! Enough!... I am between the anvil and the hammer». And some time later, on 21 March, to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino: «The storms are growing, I am right in the midst of thorns».

What had happened? Fr. Bianchi had completed the new Constitutions. The Mother had seen them and discussed them with the revisers of the S. Congregation. She had set out the reasons for her strong misgivings. She could not accept those Constitutions «because they did not meet the needs of the Institute» (Summarium, p. 751). Faithful to the Holy Spirit and obedient to the Holy Father — «Keep the spirit firm» — she tried to convince those most distinguished persons, who had so readily offered to help her, of the sacred reasons for her refusal. The case was of course suspended and all decisions postponed. But light came from another source. On 12 June 1874 the Cardinal Protector approved, by way of experiment, the printing of a text of Constitutions certainly written by Fr. Tornatore. There is good evidence that the Bishop of Piacenza, Mgr. Ranza, was not uninvolved in the decision (L M. Rosa 20.3.1874 to Rapallino and her reply 21.3.1874). Truly prophetic were the Mother's words: «And yet it will be that one, and everyone will be convinced» (L 113).

She could call herself content, after so many sorrows and «battles». Her announcement to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa is a sigh of relief: «At last we have the Rule, I will bring it to you». With equal joy the Daughters of Saint Anne took in their hands that little book, to make their own and put into practice in order to become holy.

«Today we had the reading of the Rule» (L Sr. A. V. Rapallino to the Mother: 22.6.1874).

Concerning Fr. Tornatore too the truth was making headway, and his figure reappeared in full light, upright and great in virtue, learning and holiness. He would be able to serve the Institute. Permission, first unofficial and later complete, would restore him, with all the charisms of official recognition, to the beloved Family of the holy Mother of Mary Immaculate. Cardinal Protector Giuseppe Berardi, Cardinal Vannicelli's successor, would order him to write the Constitutions to be presented to the S. Congregation to complete the approval process. The three aims of Mother Rosa's programme — approval of the Rule, her own tasks and the Father's — were at last brought together in the great aim: the consolidation and growth of God's Work. She could sing the Te Deum (L 277) and contemplate the wonderful intervention, more visible every day, in «His Work, which grows stronger every day and sails ahead in full sail» (L 266).

Criteria for this edition

The publication of the whole block of letters of 1871-1874, more than 700 in all, is required by the particular unity of the letters themselves, since they not only deal with recurring events and subjects close together in the chronological sequence of the four years, but above all because they are shot through with the important theme of the Rule. The edition is therefore one, although for plausible typographical reasons and obvious practical ones it is presented, following the first volume already published, in two volumes: Lettere 2 (1871-1872) and Lettere 3 (1873-1874). As before, the criteria of a standard scholarly edition are followed, making only strictly necessary changes to the original text: punctuation, capitals or lower case, double consonants. One or more words missing from the text but needed to understand the Mother's thought have been added in [ ], while original words of the text have been placed in ( ) because superfluous or because they make exact understanding difficult.

Also placed in [ ] are the date or missing parts of it, the recipients omitted in draft letters, and finally the dots indicating missing parts of the letters, usually at the end (conclusion or signature).

The letters are numbered in chronological order. Dates missing from the original, and the names of omitted or incomplete recipients, have been deduced through comparative contextual study with other letters and chronological and historical data.

Each letter is introduced by a summary as an overall presentation and is divided into numbered paragraphs, to present it in a more structured, clear and practical typographical form and to make it easier to locate the points cited in the notes at the foot of the individual letters or in the indexes that follow the body of letters. In citing letters within the same volume, only the letter number is given, followed by the paragraph number (e.g. L 1,2). If the reference is to the notes, the letter number is followed by the abbreviation n. (e.g. L 1, n. 2). If the citation refers to letters in earlier volumes, the volume is given first (e.g. Lettere 1, L 14,2).

The body of letters, the central and largest block of each volume, is preceded by two parts that introduce it and make it easier to approach — the presentation and the introduction — and followed by five indexes.

Taken together, these form an illuminating framework for the individual letters and the whole, since with a rich and varied fund of information and observations, both on Mother Rosa as author and protagonist and on people, facts, events, places and times, they offer the reader valuable tools for an objective and historically more exact understanding of the letters and related events. More than this: each index, in its own specific way, provides through concrete data keys for reading both the individual letters within the overall picture and the themes that run through the letters.

Further details on the function of the indexes are in Lettere 1, p. 35, to which we refer the reader.

The Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, founded four years ago, is growing, blessed by God, in the number of its Religious and in its particular activities. The Rule, already printed with the approval of the Diocesan Bishop Mgr. Ranza, has been sent to the Holy Father and to the S. Congregation. In all this the work of one of his Sons, Fr. G. B. Tornatore, has been of fundamental importance. Since his presence is therefore extremely necessary to the community, she asks him to place him under his direct obedience as Superior General, exempting him from dependence on the local Superior.

Reverend Superior General,

  1. Since the surest way is to go to the source from which grace must spring, this unworthy servant of the Lord, forgetting her nothingness, sends Your Reverence this petition to obtain what she sets out here.

  2. Four years ago1 God caused a new Institute to be born in the Church, the Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, and with the blessing of the Most High it prospers, counting a large number of Religious. There are three houses and the fourth is about to open.2 Its works are: nursing the sick of both sexes at home and in hospitals; taking in poor girls in danger of losing their virtue and giving them the Christian and moral education suited to them; a free boys' school for children of humble condition, where, when possible, they are even given a little food, as in a second nursery; perpetual adoration day and night of Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament.

  3. It has been blessed by the Church, which has granted our oratories very wide faculties.3 The Holy Father Pius IX has our Rule, as has the Sacred Congregation, which in due course will give its approval. The Common Rules have long been printed with the approval of the Diocesan, Monsignor Bishop Count Ranza,4 whose letter Your Reverence will find enclosed; he joins me in begging Your Reverence's charity to grant what I ask, humbled at your feet, since I cannot come there in person because of my poor health; and it is this that so anxiously drives me to set everything in order with God's help.

  4. All this was done by one of your sons, the Rev. Mr. Tornatore; I serve him only as a wretched instrument. He now holds the post of professor at the Alberoni College; this year the classes end,5 and nothing more is needed now than for Your Reverence to deign to send an obedience assigning him to the care of this Institute, removing him from the obedience of his local Superior so that he is subject only to Your Reverence. He is too necessary to this community.

  5. Know that we are directed by your sons,6 who received the order from the Diocesan.

  6. Grant, for charity's sake, the prayer of this poor creature who, in the name of the whole community, warmly begs Your Reverence to grant this request of mine.

May Your Reverence send your fatherly blessing to one who humbly awaits it and respectfully signs herself

Your Reverence's most humble Servant Sr. A. M. Rosa Gattorno

Good Superior,

  1. As is my duty, I come to thank you for all you did for our little Carlotta; but the outer wall formed by my sins2 prevents the Lord's grace from reaching this creature; yet in spite of this, by his great mercy it may be granted her.

  2. Good Superior, I now warmly beg you to agree to what I set out here: to raise a very special prayer to the Most High for a grace I am awaiting, and to have others pray too... — I hope you understand me —.3

  3. If my request were not too bold, I would ask you for a reply bringing me favourable news of what I am waiting for.4

She has received the accounts. She urges observance of the Rule, and in particular of silence, an indispensable means of living spousal union with Jesus.1

Our daughter,

  1. I received your letter today, with the accounts for the whole year enclosed; let us revive our trust in God and he will not fail us with his providence.

  2. Daughter, nothing frightens me or causes me the slightest worry; only one thing intimidates and frightens me: offending God, because that alone can suspend his grace. So try to observe your holy Rule, and do not let your book wear out in your pocket, but let it first imprint its indelible characters on your heart.2

  3. Try to practise strict and mitigated silence; guard these two most noble instruments, the tongue and the voice, which God gave man to praise him with, not, as happens, to displease him. Very often it happens to his Spouses that for a passing pleasure of no use we linger in frivolous talk, and meanwhile a fault against the Rule is committed, for, says the holy Mother, in the time of mitigated silence you may only speak of holy things or of necessary things belonging to your work; you will not talk about sick people you have nursed, nor about people who came to visit you, nor about relatives.3

  4. Blessed, I say, will be the Daughter of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, who forms within herself that enclosed garden into which she lets no thought enter but that of Jesus; sure that this gracious gardener, finding it empty of earthly fruits, will plant there lovely, fragrant ones, so that his beloved

Spouse may taste beforehand the delights of heaven.4 The careless Spouse who has oil and does not use it to fill her lamp, who has the sweetest perfumes and will not perfume her soul with them to remove the stench of her deadened passions, is not dear to the Eternal Father.5 My strength is failing; I must stop. God bless you; I am your poor

Mother R. G.

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I will not tell you about the journey, because you will hear about it from our Superior.2 My little daughter, is it all over? Are you happy?3

She has learned from her letter that all is going well. This should give reason for thanksgiving and resolutions to strive to «please» God and fulfil his will. God's heart is ablaze with charity. Whoever lacks charity cannot share in love or enjoy its sweetness and fruits. She should look at the image of charity in Father Tornatore: he spends himself entirely for them.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with you. Our blessed daughter,

  1. Just a line to prove to you that I always hold you in the heart of Jesus. From your last letter I see that all is going well; let us bless the Lord for it, our help, our master who teaches us so well, and let us try to profit by his lessons and be diligent, so as to please him and fully satisfy his will.

  2. My daughter, if you knew what consolation I feel just in saying these words, pleasing God, and still more when the sweet thought awakens vividly in me of being, or being able to become, his delight, I am quite beside myself, so that if I had to face the cruellest martyrdom I would feel nothing. Who can doubt it? Can there be a creature who thinks otherwise and does not feel what I say? No, I do not believe it; but if I knew there was someone who felt it more than I, I would weep and weep and would work so hard to get ahead of her.1

  3. Ah, my Eternal Father! Daughter, the heart of this God is so beautiful and so loving that no words can express it. Daughter, do you know what burns in this vast heart?

  1. How sweet it is for us when we can bring relief to someone in need, how we feel a wholly pure affection awaken in us for those creatures, however repulsive, and if our very blood were needed, we would quickly draw it from our veins to feed the poor man or the sick!3

  3. I would like to add many other things, because when I speak of charity, my daughter, it seems I would never stop; I find everything in it, every consolation — everything, in a word.5

  4. But I must stop, because I have to attend to other very urgent matters. That is what we must do: always leave our own pleasure to serve God.

Despite her many occupations she writes to prove that she constantly remembers her before God, who alone must occupy our thoughts and towards whom we must strive with all our faculties. Love of creatures lowers us; love of God makes us beautiful.1

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Our daughter,

  1. Just a line, because, as you will imagine, I am so busy that I have not a minute's rest. I do this to prove to you that I never forget you and always keep you present before God, as I wish you would do the same and come at last to understand that we must have no other object to occupy our thoughts, our heart, in short the only object of our life, but God, God alone; to live for him, crucified for him.2

  2. Daughter, what use is the whole world if we do not have God? None, less than nothing; everything belonging to this earth is dust and smoke; love of creatures is nothing but a foul contagion which, the more it grows in them, the more it gives off a stench of death, for it only deadens us and makes us true brutes, idolaters of the flesh and the senses, a horrible thing, repugnant beyond words, compared with the love of a God all most perfect and most pure, most delightful, most sweet, which the more it grows in us the more it purifies us, makes us beautiful, fragrant with a most sweet and eternal air, and nourishes our soul.3

  3. Reflect... all this, daughter, lasts for eternity. Courage: a brief suffering for an eternal joy!

  4. It would be good for you to write a couple of lines to your uncle,4 the one who comes here — you understand me — and tell him I am at S. P. d'Arena. Send the letter to me and I will forward it to him.

As Lent approaches, her mind is constantly turned to Jesus in the desert. Contemplating his sufferings, let us prepare for him a heart empty of ourselves, so that he may possess it, enrich it with every virtue and set it on fire with his divine love.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My Vincenza, now and in Eternity,

  1. Since I cannot leave these dear creatures tomorrow, Saturday, I will try to make up for my absence with this letter.1

  2. Blessed daughter, a beautiful thought fills my mind all day: that the time is drawing near when Jesus left his mother and went to begin his passion.

  3. My Vincenza, let us try, for charity's sake, to lay in a little store so that we can follow him and relieve some of his torments, especially in those forty-seven days he spent in the desert, lacking everything and exposed to such harsh weather.

  4. Nothing else can serve dear Jesus but that little care in carrying out our duties exactly.

  5. My daughter, when we are with him in this desert and see him shivering with cold, his feet bare, his head aching, half dead, without a pillow to rest his beautiful head, those wavy fair locks that look so lovely to our eyes and drew the gaze of the whole world — alas! My dear Love, how can I bear to see you lie down and lay your head on a stone? Ah, no, let my head serve you as a pillow! But no! Perhaps because of the smoke of my many disordered thoughts and the disordered appetite of my mind's senses, full as it is of pride, self-love and vainglory, all this would only make you feel the painful piercings in advance. What can I do, my good?2

  1. My Vincenza, let us empty these faculties of every earthly and perishable affection and prepare it empty, so that Jesus may not disdain to come and rest his head on ours, but accept it, rest in it and fill it with knowledge and every virtue, especially his continual presence.

  2. I live in the certainty that I shall soon see my Vincenza stripped of herself and clothed entirely with Jesus, with charity, patience, trust in God, courage and faith.3

  3. Goodbye, my daughter; this farewell I address to your body, for your spirit I mean to keep clasped with me in the Heart of Jesus, so that it may not stray but be wholly set on fire with his divine love, and I shall not be content until I see it blazing with that love.

I am your poor Mother Sr. A. M. Rosa

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter,

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I hear from the Delegate that you are not very well; for charity's sake take care of yourself, my blessed daughter; these are the caresses of our Jesus. The road to Paradise is made of thistles, but at its end are found the precious jewels of a Sovereign spouse.2

  2. To suffer in order to be much loved; suffering is a sure sign of God's love; how sweet it is to suffer and grieve for Jesus! You see, my daughter, if suffering could be stolen, I would turn thief;3 but we must be content with the little that this wretched human nature can bear, because our merciful God does not want to give more than we can comfortably bear.4

Goodbye; the Lord bless you, and believe me your poor M. Rosa

My dear, dear daughter,

I will stop here, because I shall soon tell you the rest in person.

Regarding the girl recommended by Signora Portapulia, she has told the lady the minimum monthly fee. She will write again about this and about the cost of the beds.1

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Our daughter forever,

  1. Just one line, my blessed daughter; today I received another letter in which you speak of the Portapulia matter. Poor affectionate Mother Rosa

I want this letter for the Father to be put into his own hands.

She has not answered his letter because she had to leave for Sampierdarena. As she must go to Rome, she asks him to find her lodging with some poor person. In a few days she will go to Nizza to open a new house.

A.M.F.

My good Father Agostino,

  1. Forgive me for not answering your letter, which Countess Caracciolo handed to me;1 the reason was that the next day I had to leave for S. P. d'Arena, where I still am.

  2. Father Agostino, so our hopes came to nothing; patience!2 Well then, I will come to see you, and I hope soon. Father Agostino, I would like to know where to stay, not in a religious house, for you know well that I am loaded with vices and would only give bad example; so a hovel in the house of some poor woman, as long as it is out of the public squares;3 I desire nothing but to be able to speak with the Holy Father, and then I shall be satisfied.

  3. In a few days I shall go to Nizza to occupy the great Franciscan Convent.4 Father Agostino, pray a little to the Madonna to send us plenty of providence, for we are growing moment by moment. Only the strength of this useless creature lessens every day.

  4. How many things I have to tell you — it will take a month, when I have the good fortune to speak with you.

  5. So write and tell me there will be this hut; I would not want you to put yourself out, for charity's sake; just ask some poor woman who comes begging to let me use it. Father Agostino, forgive me if I write to you too familiarly; punish me, give me a penance; anyway, this is all Arabic to me.

Bless me and always believe me. Carlotta greets you and respectfully kisses your hand

Your most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

Her health is still precarious. She is glad to hear Sr. A. Francesca is better; she should be told to treat her afflictions with more detachment and to put all her thought into loving God alone. A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Our daughter,

  1. Just a line to answer your last two letters. I will not speak of my health, for I can truly say that it is the props of your prayers that keep me from closing my eyes in the blessed eternal sleep.1 May God's will be done in this Servant of his.

  2. How it comforted me to hear of Sr. A. Francesca's improvement. For charity's sake tell her to treat the afflictions the Lord sends her, to take them more coolly;2 then she will have no more relapses; let her leave every worldly concern to God, and let all our concerns be to love him alone. For whoever thinks only of loving God, everything else becomes a fine nothing, less than nothing.3

  3. Now, blessed daughter, see how well the Father advised you about Signora Rocca.4 Yes, as soon as I arrive in Piacenza I will go to her at once and apologise for our Sister's mistake.

4. Learn from this distinguished painter who teaches you so well and sketches for you the way to Paradise; so hide nothing from him, tell him everything. And where better can we lay down all our troubles than in the hands of this holy Father, whom God has given us only out of his immense mercy? Goodbye, for I have people here.

I am your poor M. Rosa

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Vincenza, daughter, wholly ours,

  1. I am in such a hurry that I am quite flustered; they are waiting for me, and first I want to write to you so as to send it to the post.

  2. On Wednesday1 I shall be at the station at 11.30; then I can tell you everything I have no time to write now.

  3. I hope to find you well and cheerful, and wholly transformed into Saint Anne, her true disciple: her speech, her features, and finally her gaze.2

  4. There, my beloved daughter: Jesus wills it so, and so be it. Heaven is for us; one day there we shall enjoy what we long to enjoy here below.3 Yes, with me for an eternity.

I am your poor

M. Rosa

After mentioning the Institute's work for young people and for the population struck by the smallpox epidemic, she asks that a grant be decreed to meet its continual expenses.1

Most Illustrious Mayor,

  1. Since it was established in Sampierdarena,2 the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne has already twice received benefits from this illustrious Municipality.

  2. The moral education of girls of the common people and free home nursing of the sick of every condition are the Institute's chief purpose.

  3. The smallpox epidemic that afflicted this city last year and at the beginning of the present year 1871, and which by God's mercy ended a short while ago,3 brought this Institute heavy expenses: expenses to protect from the disease, as far as possible, the girls supported and educated there; expenses to maintain a greater number of religious, needed to meet the many demands and requests of the poor families struck by the dreadful illness and so to devote themselves to their welfare.

  4. Now the Institute, having no other satisfaction than that of having relieved them a little by nursing the smallpox victims, especially at night, as the Municipality well knows, and constantly aiming4 to serve the large population of Sampierdarena usefully, the undersigned Superior draws Your Lordship's attention to the work of the newborn Institute in recent times and, trusting that it will also be considered by the Aldermen of the Municipal Council, is confident that you will decree a grant for the said Institute, so that it may be relieved of the many expenses incurred for the reasons stated above.

Hoping to be heard, with sentiments of the most sincere gratitude she has the honour to sign herself, most illustrious Sir,

Your most devoted Servant Sr. A. M. Rosa Gattorno

She thanks him for his charity and sets out an urgent need. Water, so necessary, is at present drawn from a fountain ten minutes' walk away. Would he kindly have the pipes extended into the house.1

Most Illustrious Sir,

  1. I feel truly bound to tell you what I could not say aloud the other day; words failed me to thank you and to describe more vividly the extreme needs in which we find ourselves. All this I must put down to my wretchedness and to the poverty of my speech.2

  2. Now allow me to express with my pen what I feel towards Your Lordship, our good benefactor; be assured that the charity you do is so great that it gives life to poor creatures who are truly in need, especially in the most basic needs, such as water, which these poor creatures must go and fetch to drink and to cook: you know the distance, more than ten minutes.

  3. Do not abandon us; as the chief of our benefactors, you will have a special place in our prayers.

  4. Please accept our thanks, and may God pour out on you and your family his choicest blessings and repay you a hundredfold for what you do for us; and I, as the least of all, shall not forget so great a benefactor in my prayers.

Please accept, most illustrious Sir, my thanks, and believe me Your Lordship's

Most humble Sr. A. M. Rosa Gattorno

She writes in her own hand to comfort her. The road to heaven is wearisome, but at its end «suffering» turns into «joy». If it pleases God, they will be blessed together in Heaven and will pray for those who caused their sufferings.1

A.M.F.

My beloved daughter,

  1. Thank you for all the good news you give me; I have, one might say, [only just] got up, but am still not well. I am making the effort to write to you in my own hand and encourage you.2

  2. The road to heaven is very wearisome, but at its end there is a delightful garden covered with pleasant plains; there one enjoys a joy without equal, there all our suffering [is] swallowed up in as much joy. [Looking] there, yes, a ravenous hunger for suffering comes over us; why, my Daughter? Because all the suffering we have endured in this valley of tears will be rewarded with as much joy; so, a brief suffering for a long joy.3

  3. What do you think? Ah yes! Suffering, you are truly my only treasure; and whoever seeks delights here below will find them neither in this homeland nor in the other, and will be unhappy for ever.

  4. Ah, if it pleases God to take such delight, then indeed we shall sing together those beautiful hymns of glory sung by the blessed in Heaven, and we shall learn their harmonies and, rejoicing in the bliss of a God who is all love,4 happy and content we shall greet our oppressors and accusers, those who caused our suffering, and raise fervent prayers to the Most High for them, that he may give them the graces to become holy.

  5. Cheerful in sorrows; sad, sad in cheerfulness. Do we understand each other? It seems to me my Carolina answers: Yes.5 Goodbye, for it is late. I am your affectionate

Mother Sr. Anna Maria Rosa. God bless you together with the others.

One must be armed with peace and patience to be sustained in difficulties. For the problems of the house she should turn to the Father. She does not know when she can return. She has arranged for running water to be installed and a cistern built. She urges them to pray to St Joseph for providence.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter, wholly ours

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Yesterday I received your letter in which you tell me about Mr. Defilippi.1 Patience, my blessed daughter; let peace and patience be your two defenders, and try to be devoted to them and hold on to them tightly, so as never to be without their support. And believe me, when you have those two you can defy the whole world.2

  2. For everything you write to me about that house, turn to the Father.3 He will give you holy advice and will see to everything himself.

  3. I do not know when I shall return, because the affairs of this house are getting more and more entangled. I am having water put into the kitchen and also having a small cistern made for the overflow of the Nicolai water, so that the religious will no longer have to go down to the gardener's, and washing will be much easier for them.4

  4. Everyone is well except Sr. A. M. Annunciata.5 I don't know; I think she will recover, but she is very ill; let us pray. I will not go on, as I have too much to do, and you take care of yourself.

  5. Greet all the Sisters for me; have them pray to St Joseph to send us providence; he owes [us] more than anyone, because he is over the dying and we nurse them, and he must remember the fish he has caught through the Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, and this very year, and see to it that he sends us everything we need.6

Goodbye, the Lord bless you; faith, trust in God, and we shall have everything

I am your Poor Mother Rosa

She sends a letter for the Father. She must not forget to have the windows repaired. She is fairly well. She should look after her health. Sr. A. Annunciata is ill.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Our daughter, my blessed one,

  1. See that this letter of mine, enclosed here for the Father,2 reaches him at once, because it is urgent.

  2. Now please do not forget to have the carpenter make that guard for the windows, the one in her3 dormitory and the other. For charity's sake; I don't know why, my daughter, but this thought occupies me immensely.

  3. Today I am sending you some fruit — dried figs — which you will share with the other house.4 See that they are given out sensibly in the evening, because it is a fast day, but a plateful5 is not needed, because then, you will understand, about five seem enough to me for the fast. Then do as the Father tells you.

  4. I am fairly well, except for the pain in my lung that tears at me and stops me writing in the evening. Thank God, I can work a great deal, and I give this pig no rest all day and a good half of the night as well.6

  5. I hear your stomach is hurting; for charity's sake take care of yourself. Here we have Sr. A. M. Annunciata who, as far as I can see, is quite consumptive;7 she is up, but one can see that since she had erysipelas she has never been well. If she were able to make the journey and the Father agreed, I would take her to Piacenza to die,8 but I doubt she will come.

Goodbye, because it is going to the post. Give greetings; I greet you. I am your poor

She will stay a few more days until the work is finished. Everyone is expecting him for the Confirmation. After Easter they will certainly have to go to Nizza. Very Rev. Fr. Luigi,

  1. I received your esteemed letter of the 28th; I would have liked to answer at once, but my immense occupations prevent me from fulfilling even my strictest duties. I am delighted to hear of the great acclaim1 and of your good health, in spite of so much labour. Of this I had no doubt at all.

  2. Now, as is my duty, I give you news of this poor house, where I am staying a few more days to see water put into the kitchen and other little things which, on your return, you will see whether they are to your liking, always free to change them as you think best. I have tried to guess your wishes.2

  3. Everyone is waiting for you for the Confirmation; flowers and everything are being prepared; you will find fine gifts, pretty things for your Chapel. I am leaving everything in order, and when you come you will fix the day and time both for the retreat and for the feast day.

  4. Now to Nizza: after Easter we shall certainly have to go there; Fr. Luigi, in that great building and Church you will surely need to stay at least two months; tell me you will do so, helping me as you have done in this poor house.3

I have a free moment, I must carry out; I will tell you about it in person; I am afraid to write it, as it is a delicate matter of God's work; other things get known, but...5

6. So you see what a vineyard!... I shall not be content until I see you wholly taken up with the Daughters of Saint Anne, and that phrase of yours — my Parish — tell me that your Parish6 is the work of Saint Anne; I hope you will calm me with a letter assuring me that you will be all for Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate. Everyone greets you, girls and Religious, and with them I ask your Blessing and remain

Your very poor Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

She encourages her to cooperate with the Lord's action in her. He wants her on the road of suffering, which leads to pure love and conformity with his will. She will have a visit from the Bishop and should see that he finds the house in good order. She must watch the conduct of the nursing sisters, speak of it to the Father and correct them, all zeal for God's work.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. From your letter, which I received today, I see you are short of breath again; patience! My daughter, God wants you on a road along which he usually leads his beloved; it is dark, full of thistles and sorrows;2 but do you know what he does when they reach its end? He makes them drunk with his delicious wine, so that they forget themselves and in their suffering run thirstily along this road; they feel the thorns, but the pricks are sweet to them; they feel the tearing of their breast, and it is changed into loving heartbeats, because they feel nothing more, hear nothing more than a burning blaze of love that drives them to seek the beloved; and if to reach him they had to go down into the abyss of hell, they would go down into those atrocious pains, for having at last found their Good. Not even there would they feel anguish, because this Being sweetens everything, and he is the nectar inside the sharpest thorns.3

  1. So you are to have a visit from your Bishop? What are you thinking of preparing for him? Not even chairs to sit on? Hurry, go begging and buy chairs, and send to see whether the beds I ordered are ready,4 and ask the Delegate of the Dal Verme House to give you some cloth to make curtains, at least in one room, that is, the big room; and a curtain in the little room; and for the church, ask the Parish Priest's sister to lend you a church curtain at least, and then providence will come. Mind you, it really will come.5

  2. Teach your daughters what to say to him and how to receive him; try always to be in order. Go to Grandi about the tanks, for now is the time to do something; ask him for charity's sake.6 This word is very clever at entering hearts, moving them and obtaining everything.

  3. The nurses must do their duty. For charity's sake be firm and strict about this, for it is a matter of offending the Lord. Be ready to tell the Father everything, especially the nurses' faults. Cover nothing up; take care to reprove everything with great firmness and be exact in this.7 I tell you this for your guidance, not to rebuke you, nor because you do not do it, but because I truly want you to be that daughter of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, all zeal, all eyes for God's work. Is it true, my blessed daughter, that it is so? All God's, all mine for ever.8 Goodbye; believe me, in the heart of my Jesus, wholly your Poor

Mother Rosa

5. I don't know if you will be able to read it, because it is so badly written, as my stomach hurts very, very much; I have been talking at length all day.

M. [R.]

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter, wholly mine

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Two lines in haste; I am sending by Sr. A. M. Angiola1 a design that will be very useful to her for the carpet. Now I want you to send me the one for the surplice that I drew.

  2. I do not know when I can come, because things are so entangled that I really don't know how to get away. I am your Poor Mother Rosa

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

She has already offered to God the news she was sent and prayed to him for her daughters. Every pain turns into joy when one suffers for him. She urges prayer to St Joseph for providence. The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter, wholly ours

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I received a letter from you a few hours ago and am answering in my own hand, my daughter. Yesterday you will have received Sr. A. Vincenza's letter saying I would be there on Saturday, but an unexpected matter has kept me and does not allow me to fix the day.1

  2. How many things you tell me. I have already handed everything over to my God and prayed him to give you peace and strength to bear it all with holy resignation.2 My dear, what days of sorrow and pain these are; but everything turns into joy when one suffers for our Lord; they turn into sweets of paradise.3

  3. My health is somewhat better today, but I had two days of purgatory. What spasms everywhere; yesterday morning I practically had to flee from the church because I was feeling faint.

  4. How sorry I am about Giulietta;4 it seems to me that if

you had anointed her a little with the oil of the Eternal Father and fed her, treated her with linseed enemas, in short stayed by her side to restore her... Patience!

  1. I take up my pen again after two hours in the parlour. You speak to me of providence. Pray; whoever prays well obtains everything. Here St Joseph has worked truly great miracles for us, as great as he is in heaven. True, today he blocked my way to come to you, but he opened others for providence. Just to bring water to the kitchen and the girls' refectory, the cost comes to over 1,000 francs, and a hundred and 11 and a half metres of lead pipe.5

  2. Now I am having a little room made with a connecting corridor to the girls' dormitory, which will cost a good 200 francs. Finally I had the grounds fenced on all sides with wooden and iron gates, and put a big bell at the top of the drive; St Joseph saw to that too.6 The work in the Church is as beautiful as can be; all St Joseph: what a dear Saint!

  3. I think I shall come on Wednesday or Saturday of next week; certainly Wednesday, together with the Lady Sr. A. Vincenza has already written to you about.7 Tomorrow I will send you some dried fruit, figs and prunes and a few raisins. This is for visitors and Priests,8 and you are not to give any to anyone else, because you see it would take too much for the Community. It is for those ladies who will come. The curtains of the Father's alcove are old; have them mended, taking off the backing cloth.

Greet everyone for me, and believe me your affectionate

Poor Mother Sr. A. R.

She urges order and cleanliness throughout the house, especially in the kitchen, which must be whitewashed and cleaned. Improvements to the house's water supply will be needed. Money is short, but God will provide. She will return to Piacenza on the 29th.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us. Our daughter,

  1. At this moment I am in Genoa and am using this minute to write to you, so that you have time to do what I would like to find ready. Not only the guest quarters in order and clean, but the whole house, especially the kitchen, which is always so dirty; have it whitewashed; the copper pans1 well polished, all hung in the first kitchen, and the coffee pots too; in short, everything in order. This house at S. P. d'Arena looks like a drawing room, it is so bright and clean. The other day I brought a friend of mine who had arrived unexpectedly, and she said: «What lovely cleanliness; not even private houses are kept like this».2

  3. Let us hope the Lord will send us everything — he, everything, all — and to us the confusion and humiliation, the annihilation, the shame. I am truly nothing but a wretched servant of the Lord — let me write it to you this way — real dung.

Goodbye, because I want to post it; I am your

Poor Mother

5. On Wednesday the 29th of this month we shall be at the station at 11.30. Greet everyone for me; if I am not with Sr. A. Vincenza, please be kind to whoever you find with me,5 so that she is not left alone or less graciously received.

She is in great distress and poor health; she also suffered much from walking a long way to visit a benefactress. But she does not feel her sorrows, because she offers everything to the suffering Jesus. Several priests gladly come to visit her and celebrate Holy Mass in the house chapel.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My dear daughter,

  1. I hold you clasped to the Heart of Jesus, as every morning; now, [out of] the gratitude my Master and Saviour taught me, [I write you] a line which you will receive before I leave; I thank and bless you, my dear daughter, for caring about my health, which I do not deserve.

  2. If you knew what distress I am in, you would surely weep with me; but let us pour out all our tears at the feet of our dear Good and try to put them into the wound, to sweeten his bitter pains.1 Yes, my dear, Jesus suffers and my dear Eternal all, Father, God, is grieved; his anger is greatly to be feared, for he is weary of seeing his Son suffer, dear, beautiful Jesus.2

  3. Today I feel ill, and this morning I could not get out of bed for meditation, only for Mass. What spasms, what anguish I feel; God alone sees them.3 Yesterday, coming back from Genoa, where I had to take a little walk to visit a Lady who, one may say, is ill because she is so old and wanted to see me, since she is the one arranging to give us the house in Genoa — silence — I thought I would die.4 What can you do, the carriage cannot go there; that's how it is, you know, with these nobles.

  1. I am coming, but I shall not give you money; see how poor I am; I always tell you that I am nothing but a hindrance to you and good for nothing, except doing harm and causing distress; what am I coming for? To be a nuisance, for if I don't give you money, what use is it for me to come? Better leave that aside; I don't want to share my sorrows with you — in truth I don't feel them, and I give everything to my Jesus.

  2. Listen, the parish priest5 is all upset because many priests come here, and on Sundays there is always Mass, and by distinguished priests. On Sunday he was really annoyed; listen to what he said: «And how is it that all the priests have now taken to going up there? What is this business?». In these days the Jesuit Sapetti, a fine preacher, sent word to me; he knew me once when he came to the Congregation while I was still presiding, and he spoke to us; now he is entirely devoted to the Marchioness Doria and the Marchioness Gavotti.6 He said he would come and see me, but I had said I was leaving on Saturday, so there was no more time! This morning Fr. Galbarino7 came, a priest — or rather Bishop Magnasco's right hand.

  3. I'll make you laugh after Easter, because I don't feel like it now, these being days of sadness as the sufferings of our dear Jesus are renewed so vividly. How much he suffered! It grieves me!

I am your Poor M. Rosa. Greet Francesca for me

She warns the Sisters who begin the day with an act of laziness and are slow to go to the chapel for prayer. She urges mortification of gluttony, citing examples of various saints and of Jesus. We must show God by deeds our desire to love him and to enjoy the vision of the Eternal Father in Paradise.1

My daughters,

  1. To those who out of laziness are slow in the morning to answer the voice of the Lord, who calls them to his temple to speak to their heart and instil in them living maxims for doing well the work that he, through his representatives, has assigned them.23 Ah, Daughter of Saint Anne, how can you do all the other works of the day well if you began it with an act of laziness?4

  2. You have displeased your Spouse. He who with such love spent the whole night in that little room5 waiting for you, after letting you rest in a very soft bed — and you, so ungrateful, cannot sacrifice for him a little discomfort, which is as nothing compared with his immense pains and torments.6

  3. How can we suppose that our actions conform to the holy Rule? No, I shall never believe [that there is] a Religious who cannot for her Spouse abstain from certain titbits, so truly repugnant to the mind of one who wishes to run the way of perfection. To hear that someone who wears a religious habit cannot bear abstinence from gluttony, an ugly, carnal sense that drags the creature unawares to perdition, because this is our first enemy, the flesh, and once it is satisfied the rebellion of every other sense cannot fail to follow — [it pains me]!7

  1. Do you know, O unbridled creature, when all these infected faculties8 of yours torment you with their thirst to satisfy your ugly desires, are you sure you can come out [victorious] and escape falling into sin unharmed? Ah! The Saints feared this sense, kept it extremely mortified, so that, always cast down, it might never have any strength, subdued and constantly thwarted until it was deprived of all taste — and still it was never enough for them, because they always feared it!9

  2. A Saint Rose moistened her lips with gall every morning; likewise a Saint Mariana of Jesus fed on it. Saint Rose swallowed the putrid blood of a servant girl. Our holy Father St Francis went about begging for other people's leftovers in order to mortify this sense. Staying in the house of a priest who fed him too well every day, he left that dinner to go and eat leftovers from this one and that. God did not fail to turn his meal into a most delicious flavour.

  3. Let us look at the Son of God himself, who by his example taught us to practise this mortification. Whoever cannot practise it and does not try to acquire it can never be on the way of perfection, and you will find yourselves disturbed in every part of your senses.10 She will be deprived of the gift of prayer, for these two imperfections,11 joined together, make us heavy, and prayer becomes a martyrdom for you.

  4. Come, strip yourselves of these acts of laziness; give God the first sigh of your waking, showing him by deeds your desire to love him as he deserves. Be sure that the Saints practised small mortifications, knowing that through them they would gain the greater ones and above all the glory of holy Paradise. There they will possess the beautiful sight of the Eternal Father — our dear, dear Eternal Father, all for us. Yes, O Eternal Father, [deign] to bless with your right hand these creatures of your Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, she who was your consolation; so that one day these poor, though unworthy, servants of yours and daughters of your Saint Anne may form your crown up in Heaven.

Your affectionate M. Sr. A. M. Rosa Gattorno

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Daughter,

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have just received two lines from you, half a sheet of paper, together with Chini's note. I cannot understand why you are so alarmed and frightened at having opened such a letter. My daughter, don't you see that when the addresses are general you must open them — indeed it is your duty to do so? So go on opening them and acting as you do. Hurry along as much as you can the coming of those two sisters.1

  2. Now, my dear daughter, I want you to be strong and full of trust in God. I want one thing from you: that you strive to love God with a love that is wholly pure and ardent, aflame. If you reach that, I will tell you: «Do as you will, for you will do everything well». Love and do what you will, said St Augustine. Yes, my dear, love, love this dear God the Father, and you will do everything gladly.

  3. Taking up again these two badly strung-together lines I am writing you — see, when I was a third of the way through, at the words «love my Eternal all», ah, what happened to me!! Daughter, this shattered humanity was cruelly wounded with a knife with a very thin blade. Alas! While I felt its sting — but when the cut was opened so harshly in me, ah, Daughter, what joy this most unworthy mother of yours felt!!2

  4. Courage! Ah yes! What a consoling thing it is when we can open our breast to dear God, our sovereign and all, and say to him: «Deign to look at our wounds», and number them all one by one, and the one that still bleeds and, being so open and torn, causes3 extreme pain — that is where his gaze rests. What does this most holy gaze do, my blessed daughter? It treats it with a healing balm, and the pain is stilled, and it pours over the others its sweetest, most delicious nectar, which sweetens everything, and from harsh and painful wounds they become sweetest comforts, gentle companions, loving sisters.

  5. Alas, my dear! When I speak of these wounds and remember the sweetest nectar they produce, I would do nothing but speak of them for a hundred years, never tiring or having enough; but to my great regret I must stop and deal with the affairs of this house.

  6. Now I have received your other letter, in which you tell me about the girl.4 The Father says5 that if your first note is enough for her, well and good; otherwise you can do nothing more for her; this is what your Superiors write to you. Goodbye, I am your Poor

Mother Rosa

  2. Now that I can barely gather enough strength to write you these two badly strung-together lines, I hasten to tell you everything.

  3.   1. Forgive such boldness, and as soon as my strength allows I shall come and do my duty.

All the good she has done she must attribute to Saint Anne, who will reward her. Gentleness opens hearts and disposes them to love Jesus. The Daughters of Saint Anne must be adorned with this virtue, and with sincere humility. She should move Sr. A. M. Paola to another room if she thinks it right. The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have received your two letters; today it was a great consolation to hear of the fine welcome you received from our Pastor.2 May God bless the holy hand of this holy Prelate. I am also glad to hear the teacher has arrived.

  2. My daughter, Saint Anne, our dear Mother, will reward you [for] all you have done; all is well. Believe me, my daughter, gentleness is a powerful weapon for winning hearts and leading them to love Jesus.3 It is also what keeps a community fragrant, spreading its perfume to the people who come near us;4 indeed I am of the opinion that we poor Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, more than any others must be adorned with it, because, being constantly in contact with outsiders, we need to leave in them, every time we speak with them, the liveliest impressions of delight in religion, and satisfied that everything we do is for that God who is our every consolation.

  1. How lovely it is to see in the parlour a Religious whose modest bearing goes with a gentleness and humility so sincere, not at all affected or studied, but composed, with simply a cheerful, gracious face, without grimaces; she always tries to be composed, but only because she is adorned with these virtues. She easily hides every sorrow and discomfort, but in front of everyone she always remains cheerful and content, to show others that the religious spirit is a comfort and the true rest of our souls.5

  2. Now let us turn to the house, because, my blessed creature, it is late and I am very tired from talking so much. Being sure that I speak with the word and will of my Superior,6 I would do this: if you think it is the damp that may harm Sr. A. M. Paola's health, you can put her in the Father's room, with you; but I do not mean this as an order. As for you, do as you think best; I suggest it thinking it may please you, but you must not be upset, because I leave you entirely free to do as you think best.7

  3. I forgot to write to the Father that yesterday, the second day after my arrival, Mr. della Valle8 came to see me and said it would be good for me to take Annunciata away, because it must be the air that does not agree with her.   4. Back to you: send me two sacks of maize, but at once; the Delegate asks you to send her a few pullets for eggs; it seems a pity to me to send the ones you have at home; what do you think? Do as you think best; don't worry about it, there is time; but the maize, yes, at once.

  5. What fine gifts they received these days for the church, what beautiful, costly fabrics! Maria is preparing everything new and beautiful for the coming of the Father, who is awaited like the Messiah.9 When he comes they will surely smother him with welcomes.

  6. I hear your stomach is hurting. For charity's sake take care of yourself; do not fast; eat regularly and meat, always, because I believe the Father will agree with me; I believe this is his wish. The same for poor Maddalena:10 yes, let her eat meat, since she can; for the others do as I told you: let them go to the Father. He will hear about their ailments and give them whatever dispensations he thinks best.

9. Goodbye; the Lord bless you, fill you with graces and make you holy; this poor Mother of yours clasps you forever in the Heart of Jesus; every morning she asks her God to consume her daughter Sr. A. M. Adelaide in this volcano. P.S. I repeat what I wrote to you about Sr. A. M. Paola; it would be my wish; if you do it I shall be grateful. Goodbye.

[M. Rosa]
